'''Harira''' ({{langx|ar|الحريرة|al-ḥarīra}}) is a traditional [[North Africa|North African]] soup prepared in [[Morocco]], [[Tunisia]], [[Algeria]], [[Libya]]<ref>{{cite web |title=HARIRA definition and meaning |url=https://www.collinsdictionary.com/dictionary/english/harira |website=[[Collins English Dictionary]] |access-date=25 November 2025 |language=en |date=24 November 2025}}</ref> and of Andalusian and Amazigh North African origin,<ref name="brill_60748">{{Cite web |title=Best of Delectable Foods and Dishes from al-Andalus and al-Maghrib: A Cookbook by Thirteenth-Century Andalusi Scholar Ibn Razīn al-Tujībī (1227–1293)|url= https://brill.com/display/title/60748 |publisher=Brill.com |journal=Encyclopédie berbère |language=fr |issue=17 |pages=2643–2644 |doi=10.4000/encyclopedieberbere.2156 |issn=1015-7344|doi-access=free }}</ref> with many variations, the best-known being Moroccan harira. Harira is popular as a starter, and is also eaten on its own as a light snack. It is mostly served during [[Ramadan]], although it can be made throughout the year.<ref name="Berry2012">{{cite book|last=Berry|first=Vava|title=Soup: fresh, healthy recipes bursting with seasonal flavour|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2pq_CAAAQBAJ&pg=PT130|year=2012|publisher=Pavilion Books|location=London|isbn=978-1-909108-50-9|page=66}}</ref>

It is also part of a wider [[Maghrebi cuisine]], where lemon juice and egg are added.<ref>{{cite web |title=Recipe: How to make harira |website=Jewish Journal |date=12 March 2015 |url=https://jewishjournal.com/culture/food/164439/recipe-how-to-make-harira/}}</ref>

The origin of harira is disputed. While Jewish food historian Gil Marks attributes its origin to Morocco, this claim is compelling but debatable. According to [[Algérie Poste]] and [[Andalusi Scholar Ibn Razīn al-Tujībī]],  harira is an authentic Maghreb dish of Andalusian origin and identifies it as one of the best-known dishes of Morocco and western Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, where it is traditionally associated with Ramadan.<ref name="brill_60748"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plats Traditionnels - Algérie Poste |url=https://www.poste.dz/philately/s/1464 |publisher=Algérie Poste |language=fr}}</ref> Note that Moroccan Harira differs significantly from Algerian (Western Algeria), Tunisian, and Libyan Harira. Moroccan Harira relies heavily on a dense tomato, lentil, and chickpea base seasoned with ginger, cinnamon, cilantro, and thickened with flour; while also adding some pieces of chicken or lamb to the mix. In contrast, Algerian Harira—such as (Harira Oranaise) often incorporates distinct local elements like frik (cracked green wheat) or a slightly fermented flour starter (khmira baldiya). Meanwhile, Tunisian Harira is typically centered around lamb, tomatoes, and chickpea paste, uniquely thickened with crushed caraway seeds, dried mint, and fine semolina or pasta (langue d'oiseau) rather than flour. Libyan Harira, often referred to locally simply as (Sharba Libiya) or (Hror), leans into a robust, fiery profile dominated by generous amounts of paprika, chili, garlic, and dried mint, combined with lamb, chickpeas, and a distinct tomato base.
